crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: The AI enablement audit in an investment firm examines how artificial intelligence is introduced, approved, used, and monitored across the investment lifecycle.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing is the practice of checking whether credit decisions, pricing, marketing, and servicing treat applicants and borrowers fairly regardless of protected characteristics such as race, ethnicity, sex, age, or national origin.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how an AI system reaches its outputs into language and evidence that non-specialists can assess.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information covers the rules and practices that keep confidential, price-sensitive facts about a company or its securities from being used in trading.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced means checking the output of an AI system against the purpose it was meant to serve, the sources it relied on, and the rules that apply to its use.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk covers the work of proving that an AI system used in finance is doing what it claims, and that the people responsible can show their reasoning to someone outside the firm. In practice this means running enablement audits before tools go live, testing lending models for disparate impact, writing explanations that satisfy examiners and clients, keeping material non-public information out of model inputs and outputs, and checking what a model actually produced before anyone acts on it. The work is procedural and documentary rather than mathematical: logs, test sets, approval chains, and written rationales. It sits where model engineering meets compliance, internal audit, and legal review, and it is usually triggered by a regulator, an internal policy, or a deal that requires diligence.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Bias testing has the most settled methods, with established statistical tests for disparate impact and a body of enforcement history behind them, though translating those tests to complex models remains contested. Model explanation is partly solved for simple, well documented models and largely unsolved for large ones, where explanations are approximations that can be stable, plausible, and still wrong. Data loss prevention around material non-public information is a mature discipline for text and email, and much less mature for prompts, embeddings, and model outputs that leave a firm. Output verification is the weakest area: there is no general method for confirming that a generated figure, citation, or summary is correct, so most firms rely on human review, sampling, and narrow automated checks. The honest limit across all five areas is that governance produces evidence of process, not proof of correctness, and no audit can certify that a model will behave the same way on data it has not seen.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from preparation to testing to explanation to containment to verification. The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms is the entry point, describing how a firm inventories tools, assigns owners, and sets controls before deployment, and it frames the rest of the section. Fair Lending and Bias Testing goes deep on one regulated outcome, covering test design, reference populations, and how results are documented. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients addresses the communication problem, including what can and cannot be claimed about a model's reasoning. Protecting Material Non-Public Information covers the boundary around inputs and outputs, from prompt hygiene to vendor handling. Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop at the point of use, asking how a person or system confirms an output before it enters a decision. A reader new to the area should start with the audit page, a compliance officer will want the bias testing and explanation pages, and anyone deploying a tool that touches confidential data should read the last two together.
